title: Factorising a difference of two squares
log: 2026-11-12T12:44:22Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest bank card, mat-perfect-squares-difference-two, teaches expanding the difference of two squares rather than factorising it, and mat-expanding-factorising covers that factorising step only as one of several broader techniques, so neither matches this point exactly.

draft.title: Factorising a difference of two squares
card: A difference of two squares is one perfect square minus another, such as \(x^{2} - 25\). Here \(x^{2}\) is the square of \(x\), and 25 is the square of 5.
It factorises into a pair of brackets with the same two terms, one with a plus and one with a minus: \(a^{2} - b^{2} = (a + b)(a - b)\).
Example: \(x^{2} - 25 = (x + 5)(x - 5)\). Take the square root of each term, then write one plus and one minus.
Check by expanding: the middle terms \(-5x\) and \(+5x\) cancel. The pattern needs a minus between the squares. A sum such as \(x^{2} + 25\) does not factorise this way.
draft.remember: Square root of each term, then one bracket with a plus and one with a minus.

a.q: Which is the factorised form of \(x^{2} - 49\)?
a.why: 49 is the square of 7, so the brackets hold \(x\) and 7, one with a plus and one with a minus. \((x - 7)(x - 7)\) is tempting, but it expands to \(x^{2} - 14x + 49\), which has a middle term.
a.clue: What number multiplied by itself gives 49?

b.q: Which is the factorised form of \(9x^{2} - 16\)?
b.why: \(9x^{2}\) is the square of \(3x\), and 16 is the square of 4. So the answer is \((3x + 4)(3x - 4)\). Using 9 and 16 in the brackets is the tempting mistake: the brackets hold the square roots, not the squares.
b.clue: Take the square root of \(9x^{2}\), not just of the number 9.
